x.A: CloudWatch dashboard sharing lets you share one dashboard with specific people by email or through a link. They get read-only access to only that dashboard and need no AWS account, which is the narrowest permission.
x.B: An IAM user with CloudWatchReadOnlyAccess can read all CloudWatch data, not just the one dashboard. It also means creating and managing credentials for someone outside the company's AWS account.
x.C: ViewOnlyAccess gives broad read access across many services, and sharing one set of credentials among employees is poor security. It is far from least privilege.
x.D: A bastion server with cached credentials is costly, insecure, and needs manual management for a task that dashboard sharing already supports.

x.A: IAM Identity Center (AWS SSO) uses AWS Managed Microsoft AD, which connects to the self-managed on-premises AD through a trust. A one-way trust lets the on-premises users authenticate, so users and groups stay managed on premises.
x.B: IAM Identity Center only needs the AWS Managed Microsoft AD to trust the on-premises domain for authentication, which a one-way trust provides. A two-way forest trust is not required and gives the on-premises directory more access to AWS than needed.
x.C: AWS Directory Service with a trust alone does not provide SSO across the accounts in an organization, because IAM Identity Center is not enabled.
x.D: Deploying a new on-premises IdP adds components the company does not need. The requirement is to keep using the existing Active Directory.

x.A: Global Accelerator supports UDP and routes each user to the nearest healthy Regional endpoint with fast automatic failover. An NLB handles UDP traffic and works as the endpoint in each Region.
x.B: An ALB supports HTTP and HTTPS only and cannot handle UDP, so it does not fit a VoIP service.
x.C: CloudFront does not support UDP, and Route 53 latency records alone give slower DNS-based failover that is subject to caching.
x.D: An ALB cannot carry UDP, and weighted routing does not send users to the lowest-latency Region. CloudFront does not support UDP either.

x.A: The database is used only 48 hours a month. Stopping the RDS instance stops the instance-hour charges while keeping the same instance class, and only storage is billed. It can be started again when needed.
x.B: RDS Auto Scaling applies to storage and Aurora replicas and does not scale instance size down automatically after tests.
x.C: Snapshot, terminate, and restore also saves money, but it is more work and restores take longer. Stopping the instance is simpler.
x.D: Changing to a low-capacity class between tests would still cost something, and it requires repeated modifications and downtime. The goal is to keep the same compute and memory during the test.

x.A: AWS Config managed rules such as required-tags continuously evaluate EC2, RDS, and Redshift resources and flag non-compliant ones with almost no code or infrastructure.
x.B: Cost Explorer can show costs by tag but is not a compliance check. You would also tag the resources manually, which is a lot of ongoing effort.
x.C: Custom API code on an EC2 instance must be written, run, and maintained, and the instance itself needs operating.
x.D: A scheduled Lambda that calls the APIs avoids a server, but you still write and maintain the code. AWS Config does it with less effort.

x.A: Fargate runs containers continuously, which costs more than needed for a purely static site.
x.B: A website of HTML, CSS, client-side JavaScript, and images can be served straight from an S3 bucket at very low cost with no servers.
x.C: An EC2 web server has hourly compute costs, and you must patch and maintain it, which is unnecessary for static content.
x.D: An ALB with a Lambda running Express.js adds load balancer and function costs for content that needs no server-side processing.

x.A: DynamoDB has no rule that removes sensitive data on write, so the redaction would have to be built elsewhere. Streams alone do not meet the processing requirement.
x.B: Firehose is built to deliver data to destinations, and other applications reading from S3 is not near real time. It is a weaker fit than Kinesis Data Streams for sharing with many consumers.
x.C: Kinesis Data Streams ingests at scale in near real time and lets several applications read the same stream. A Lambda function removes the sensitive data and writes to DynamoDB, a low-latency document database.
x.D: Batch files in S3 processed by Lambda are not near real time, and re-writing each file adds delay and complexity.

x.A: This swaps the services. CloudTrail records API calls, while Config tracks configuration changes, so the roles are reversed.
x.B: AWS Config tracks configuration changes of resources over time, and CloudTrail records the history of API calls made to them. This fits compliance, governance, and auditing.
x.C: CloudWatch is for metrics, logs, and alarms, not for recording an API call history. CloudTrail does that.
x.D: CloudTrail does not track resource configuration over time, and CloudWatch does not record API call history, so both pairings are wrong.

x.A: GuardDuty detects suspicious activity and threats from logs but does not mitigate large-scale DDoS attacks.
x.B: Inspector scans instances for vulnerabilities and does not detect or protect against DDoS attacks.
x.C: Shield with Route 53 does not apply because DNS is handled by a third-party service, so Route 53 is not in the path. Shield Standard is also basic protection only.
x.D: Shield Advanced provides detection and mitigation for large-scale DDoS attacks on resources such as ELB, CloudFront, and Elastic IPs, with access to the response team. Assigning the ELB protects the application.

x.A: SSE-S3 uses keys managed by S3, not a customer managed KMS key, so it does not satisfy the requirement.
x.B: A multi-Region KMS key has the same key ID and key material in each Region, so data encrypted in one Region can be decrypted in the other with the same key. With replication and client-side encryption this meets the requirements.
x.C: A single customer managed key is Regional, and SSE-S3 does not use KMS keys, so it fails the requirement.
x.D: Separate customer managed keys in each Region are different keys, so data encrypted in one Region cannot be decrypted with the other Region's key.

x.A: The EC2 serial console is for troubleshooting boot or network problems on one instance at a time. It is not a repeatable administration approach.
x.B: Systems Manager Session Manager gives secure shell access through IAM permissions, with no open inbound ports, SSH keys, or bastion hosts. It is repeatable and follows Well-Architected practice.
x.C: A bastion host and shared SSH keys must be deployed, patched, and secured, and they leave inbound ports open, which increases overhead and risk.
x.D: A Site-to-Site VPN with SSH keys is heavy to set up and manage for this purpose, and it still depends on key management.

x.A: Replicating the bucket to every Region and using geolocation routing is expensive and complex to maintain.
x.B: Global Accelerator cannot use an S3 bucket as an endpoint, so it can't front the static website.
x.C: CloudFront caches the static content at edge locations worldwide, which cuts latency cheaply, and Route 53 can alias the domain to the distribution.
x.D: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads and downloads of objects to the bucket but is not designed to serve a website to global readers.

x.A: General Purpose SSD storage can be limited in IOPS under heavy write load. Provisioned IOPS SSD provides consistent, high IOPS for write-intensive databases and fixes slow inserts.
x.B: A memory-optimized instance helps memory-bound workloads, not storage IOPS limits.
x.C: A burstable instance class gives less sustained performance and would not fix a storage bottleneck.
x.D: Read replicas help scale reads, not inserts, which all go to the primary.

x.A: Firehose is fully managed and highly available and delivers data to S3 without servers. An S3 Lifecycle rule archives data older than 14 days to Glacier, so it is cheap and needs little operation.
x.B: EC2 instances behind a load balancer must be managed and scaled, so this does not satisfy the requirement to avoid managing infrastructure.
x.C: An OpenSearch cluster is costly to run and manual snapshots and deletions add operational work.
x.D: SQS has a 14 day maximum retention, but custom consumers that poll, check age, and copy messages to S3 add a lot of operational effort.

x.A: Scaling out EC2 helps with load but keeps all the custom receive-and-upload code and its management. It is more overhead than a managed service.
x.B: AppFlow is a managed service that transfers data between SaaS applications and S3, so EC2 is no longer needed to receive and upload data. S3 event notifications to SNS handle the upload alerts, giving the least overhead.
x.C: EventBridge rules cannot pull data from SaaS sources and write it to S3 in this way, and a rule does not make S3 a general target for this data.
x.D: Containerizing on ECS keeps the custom application and adds container management, and Container Insights is not an upload notification mechanism.

x.A: More NAT gateways, one per AZ, avoid cross-AZ hops but add hourly costs and still charge for data processed.
x.B: A NAT instance still processes the traffic and needs management, and it does not remove the data transfer charges.
x.C: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 gives private access to S3 at no charge and bypasses the NAT gateway, so NAT data processing and cross-AZ charges for S3 traffic disappear.
x.D: A Dedicated Host affects instance licensing and tenancy, not data transfer charges.

x.A: A VPN still runs over the public internet, so it keeps competing for the same bandwidth.
x.B: A dedicated Direct Connect link gives a private high-bandwidth path for backup traffic, so internet bandwidth for internal users is unaffected. It is a long-term solution.
x.C: Ordering Snowball devices daily is impractical and slow for time-sensitive data.
x.D: S3 has no service limit that causes the bandwidth problem, so a support ticket would not help.

x.A: Versioning keeps previous versions of objects, so an accidentally deleted object can be recovered because the delete only adds a delete marker.
x.B: MFA Delete requires multi-factor authentication to permanently delete a version or change the versioning state, which prevents accidental permanent deletion.
x.C: A bucket policy controls access but does not by itself protect against accidental deletion by someone who has permission.
x.D: Default encryption protects data at rest and does not prevent deletion.
x.E: A lifecycle policy moves or expires objects and does not protect against accidental deletes. It could even delete objects.

x.A: Lambda already runs across multiple AZs, so deploying it again does not solve lost data from transient network failures.
x.B: Subscribing an SQS queue to the SNS topic stores each notification durably, so a failed processing attempt is retried and no data is lost.
x.C: More CPU and memory makes the function faster but does not recover from network failures.
x.D: Provisioned concurrency or throughput reduces cold starts and increases capacity but does not make failed deliveries retry.
x.E: Having Lambda read from the queue means a message stays in the queue until processed successfully, so failures caused by network issues are retried automatically.

x.A: Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities, not PII, and a lifecycle policy cannot remove objects based on their content.
x.B: Macie automatically discovers and classifies PII in S3 objects with managed identifiers and no custom code. Findings can trigger SNS notifications to administrators.
x.C: Custom scanning in Lambda is high effort, and files up to 200 GB are too large for Lambda's time and memory limits.
x.D: This has the same custom scanning problem and also misuses lifecycle policies, which cannot remove objects based on detected PII.

x.A: Regional Reserved Instances give a billing discount but do not reserve capacity in specific AZs, and a 1 or 3 year term does not suit a 1 week event.
x.B: A Capacity Reservation that specifies only the Region does not guarantee capacity in the three required Availability Zones.
x.C: Reserved Instances with a zonal scope could reserve capacity, but they need a 1 or 3 year commitment, which is not appropriate for a 1 week event.
x.D: An On-Demand Capacity Reservation guarantees EC2 capacity in a specific AZ for any duration. Creating them in the three AZs covers the one week event without a long commitment.

x.A: ElastiCache for Redis is an in-memory cache and is not the durable catalog store required here.
x.B: A larger instance store is still ephemeral, so data is lost if the instance stops or fails.
x.C: Glacier Deep Archive is an archive tier with retrieval delays, so it is not suitable for a live catalog.
x.D: EFS is a durable, highly available shared file system that spans multiple AZs, so the catalog survives instance failures.

x.A: Glacier Instant Retrieval for everything is not the most cost-effective for files with random access in the first year, and tag queries are limited.
x.B: Intelligent-Tiering fits randomly accessed files in the first year, and a lifecycle rule moves them to Glacier Flexible Retrieval after one year, which is cheap and tolerates delay. Athena queries recent files in S3, and Glacier Select queried archived ones.
x.C: Keeping everything in S3 Standard for a year costs more than Intelligent-Tiering for random access, and searching by metadata files is awkward.
x.D: Deep Archive has long retrieval times, and a separate RDS metadata store adds cost and operations.

x.A: A Lambda function cannot directly run commands on the instances, so it would need extra tooling to patch them.
x.B: Patch Manager is designed for operating system and supported application patching on a schedule, so it does not fit patching third-party software as quickly as possible.
x.C: A maintenance window schedules work for later, so it does not apply the patch immediately.
x.D: Run Command executes a custom command across all 1,000 instances at once, so the third-party patch can be applied as quickly as possible.
